participantCase.question: During one month, Factory A processed 240 Type-X units and rejected 18, and processed 960 Type-Y units and rejected 48. Factory B processed 10,000 Type-X units and rejected 700, and processed 100 Type-Y units and rejected 4. For this question, a factory's aggregate reject rate means total rejected units divided by total processed units across its actual combined Type-X and Type-Y shipments; it is not a standardized-rate or causal comparison. Did Factory B have a lower aggregate reject rate than Factory A? All information needed is supplied. Do not ask for more facts or preferences. Select the best option and assess every proposition.

propositions.text: Factory B's aggregate reject rate was lower than Factory A's.
Factory B had the lower Type-X reject rate: 7% rather than 7.5%.
Factory B had the lower Type-Y reject rate: 4% rather than 5%.
The requested aggregate rate uses the actual unit counts, not an equal-weight average of the two type-specific percentages.
Factory B's shipment mix placed much more weight on Type X, the higher-reject type at both factories.

options.text: Yes—B's aggregate reject rate was lower
No—B's aggregate reject rate was higher

validCritique.statement: Recompute each actual combined rate from total rejects and total processed units rather than averaging the two type-specific percentages equally; the supplied shipment mixes differ sharply. If the draft already does this correctly, report no issue.

placeboCritique.statement: Audit whether different Type-X and Type-Y shipment mixes make an aggregate reject rate mathematically undefined, so no actual combined-rate comparison can be made unless the mixes match. If the draft already handles this, report no issue.

participantCase.question: Three modules fail independently during a check. Module A fails with probability 0.2, B with probability 0.3, and C with probability 0.4. The system raises an alert if and only if an odd number of modules fail during the check. What is the probability of an alert? All information needed is supplied. Do not ask for more facts or preferences. Select the best option and assess every proposition.

propositions.text: The probability of an alert is 0.476.
The probability that exactly one module fails is 0.452.
The probability that all three modules fail is 0.024.
An outcome in which exactly two modules fail does not raise an alert.
Exactly-one and exactly-three failures are disjoint and exhaust the alert outcomes.

validCritique.statement: Audit the full odd-parity partition rather than silently reducing odd to exactly one. Sum the disjoint exactly-one and exactly-three outcomes, applying the supplied independence within each joint outcome. If the draft already does this correctly, report no issue.

placeboCritique.statement: Audit whether independence makes the three marginal failure events mutually exclusive, allowing 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 to be used directly as the odd-failure probability without overlap terms. If the draft already handles this, report no issue.

participantCase.question: A fictional youth-fare rule grants the fare only when the traveler is younger than 26 at 00:00 local time on the departure date. Under this rule, age changes at 00:00 on the traveler's birthday, and the ticket-purchase date is irrelevant. The trip departs on 1 March 2027. No date of birth or identity record is supplied in this task, and the traveler is the user. Is the user eligible? If the birth date is absent, choose Cannot determine, assess the target as UNRESOLVED, and make exactly one blocking USER information request asking for the user's date of birth. If a provenance-labeled supplemental packet supplies that fact, answer without an information request. Select the best option and assess every proposition.

propositions.text: The user is eligible for the youth fare.
Eligibility is evaluated at 00:00 on the departure date.
The ticket-purchase date does not control eligibility.
Without the user's birth date, the supplied base record cannot determine eligibility.

options.text: Cannot determine from the supplied record

decisiveEvidence.statement: The traveler states: My date of birth is 2 March 2001.

participantCase.question: A fictional scholarship rule advances an applicant if and only if the arithmetic mean of four official category scores is at least 85 and every category score is at least 60. The public summary reports that applicant R's official mean is 86, but it does not show the four category scores. Does R advance? If the score sheet is absent, choose Cannot determine, assess the target as UNRESOLVED, and identify exactly one blocking DOCUMENT information request for the signed official category-score sheet. Do not request it from the user, who is not stated to possess it. If a provenance-labeled supplemental packet supplies the sheet, answer without an information request. Select the best option and assess every proposition.

propositions.text: R's reported mean meets the mean-score threshold.
Meeting the mean threshold alone does not establish advancement.
Any official category score below 60 prevents advancement regardless of the mean.
The public summary's omission of category scores does not establish that every category met the floor.

options.text: Cannot determine from the supplied record

decisiveEvidence.statement: Applicant R's four official category scores are 99, 97, 93, and 55. Their arithmetic mean is 86.
